Class E surface area
Class D

A restricted area

Class E floor at 1,200 ft AGL or greater
Class B airspace around a major hub airport

Correct. The Chart User's Guide uses a faded blue vignette to show the boundary where Class E airspace with a floor of 1,200 ft AGL or higher abuts Class G, with the shaded band on the uncontrolled side of the line.

700 ft AGL
1,200 ft AGL
14,500 ft MSL

Wrong. 700 ft AGL is a designated floor, charted as a faded magenta vignette around airports with instrument approaches. It applies only inside that vignette, so it is an exception, not the floor where nothing else is designated.

Wrong. 1,200 ft AGL is also a designated floor: federal airways and areas charted with a faded blue vignette. Over much of the country it is common, but it exists only where it is designated, so it is not the answer for airspace that has no designation.

Ceiling 41,000 ft MSL over floor 13,000 ft MSL
4,100 ft AGL over 1,300 ft AGL
Ceiling over floor, hundreds of feet, MSL, last two zeros dropped. Convert to AGL by subtracting terrain elevation.

Wrong because it adds three zeros instead of two. Sectional airspace figures drop exactly two zeros, so 41 is 4,100 and not 41,000; nothing on a VFR sectional is charted in the flight levels.

About 1,200 ft AGL
About 1,700 ft AGL

Wrong because it reads the 12 as AGL. That applies the chart's AGL convention to the wrong symbol: AGL belongs to obstruction heights in parentheses, the Class E vignette floors and MTR altitudes, not to Class B, C or D limits.
Wrong because it adds the terrain instead of subtracting it. The charted floor is already measured from sea level, so the ground elevation must come off it, not be stacked on top.

The airspace extends to the surface
A surface friction advisory for the runway
Special flight conditions

About 8,100 ft

The controlling agency that schedules the area
All pilots operating in the area
ATC

Wrong. 1090 MHz is the ADS-B Out extended squitter downlink used by transponder equipped aircraft, with 978 MHz UAT as the other ADS-B link. It is surveillance data about aircraft position, not a controller to aircraft command channel.

Left turns
Right turns
Varies by aircraft

Airport advisory practices where no tower is operating

Jupiter
Jackson

Runway length in hundreds of feet
Wind speed

UA.II.B.K4e
A laser illumination incident should be reported to whom?
No one, unless the beam caused an injury
The FAA and local law enforcement
The manufacturer

AIM 7-6-13 directs pilots to report illumination events even when the flight continues normally, because the report is what warns other aircraft in the area and starts the investigation; lasing an aircraft is also a federal crime, so silence destroys the enforcement trail.

Correct. AIM 7-6-13, Laser Operations and Reporting Illumination of Aircraft, has the crew notify ATC or the FAA (the agency collects the event through its Laser Safety Initiative and the Laser Beam Exposure Questionnaire) and law enforcement handles the criminal side, since the ground source has to be located by police.

Wrong. This treats an outside hazard like an equipment defect. The manufacturer has no role in a laser event: nothing on your aircraft malfunctioned, and a vendor report reaches neither the FAA's hazard database nor the police who can find the person with the laser.

Smoke in the shot looks unprofessional to the client
Invisible violent turbulence and rising heated air

AIM 7-6-16, Flight Operations in the Vicinity of Exhaust Plumes (Smoke Stacks and Cooling Towers)

A light, low wing loading sUAS is upset far more easily than the manned aircraft the paragraph was written for.

Wrong. This is the "if it's dangerous it must be prohibited" misconception: no part 107 rule and no charted restriction bans flight near a stack or cooling tower. It is a hazard you must identify and avoid yourself when you assess the operating area, not a boundary someone drew for you.
An exhaust plume is an invisible vertical column of turbulent rising air, so avoid it laterally and never overfly a stack or cooling tower.

Radio interference from the power lines

Wires attract lightning strikes to nearby aircraft

UA.II.B.K4d
Precipitation static causes what?
Radio noise or loss of comms, and corona discharge
Longer battery life from the extra stored charge
Better GPS accuracy as the charge boosts the signal

Radio interference. Flying through rain, snow, dust or ice crystals builds an electrostatic charge on the airframe that bleeds off as corona discharge, adding radio noise that can degrade or cut communication (AIM 7-6-12).

Correct. Wrong. This treats static charge as stored usable energy. The charge sits on the airframe and bleeds off as discharge; it never feeds the battery, and there is no mechanism in AIM 7-6-12 or anywhere else by which static accumulation extends endurance.

Wrong. It has the sign backwards. Static discharge adds broadband radio frequency noise, which degrades reception, so navigation and GPS signal quality gets worse in a P static environment, not better.

An onboard crew cannot see a drone operating below the basket
A suspension device, payload or trailing antenna may hang below
Its transmitters emit radiation that can disrupt the C2 link

Correct. A free balloon has no tether; that is a moored balloon.

Wrong. This invents a hazard. The payloads are weather and research instrument packages, and neither AIM 7-6-5 nor part 101 identifies emissions or link interference as the risk; the stated risk is collision with the suspension gear or antenna below the balloon.
Never fly under an unmanned free balloon, because you must assume a nearly invisible suspension line or trailing antenna hangs below it.

No maintenance is required until something breaks
Develop and follow your own scheduled protocol
Wait for an FAA inspection

Records are unnecessary because part 107 requires no logbook
Keep maintenance, repair and part replacement records
Keep accident records only, for FAA reporting

UA.V.C.K2d
A pack ignites during charging in your garage. What is the correct immediate response?
Cover it with a wool blanket to starve it of oxygen
Douse it with plenty of water, then evacuate
Move it into a cardboard box and carry it outside

Flood it with large amounts of water or another non-alcoholic liquid to cool the pack and stop cell to cell thermal runaway, and clear the toxic smoke. Do not cover the pack, do not use ice, and do not pick it up or move it (SAFO 09013, SAFO 25002). FAA guidance does not endorse Class D agents for lithium-ion packs. A Halon, Halon replacement or water extinguisher can knock the flames down first, but only cooling with water stops thermal runaway.
SAFO 25002, Lithium Battery Fire and Overheating Conditions; SAFO 09013, Fighting Fires Caused by Lithium Type Batteries (both referenced by FAA-S-ACS-10B for UA.V.C.K2d)

Wrong, and actively harmful. SAFO 09013 states "Do not cover the device or use ice to cool the device," because a blanket or ice insulates the pack, traps the heat and makes the remaining cells more likely to go into thermal runaway. Smothering works on an oxygen fed fire, and a venting lithium cell supplies its own.

Correct. SAFO 09013 has two phases: knock the flame down with an extinguisher (Halon, Halon replacement or water based), then douse the pack with water or other non alcoholic liquid to cool the cells and keep the rest from reaching thermal runaway. Evacuating matters because the vented gases are toxic, and SAFO 25002 reinforces the overall risk.

Wrong on two counts. SAFO 09013 is explicit: "Do not attempt to pick up and move a smoking or burning device," since the pack can vent or rupture in your hands, and cardboard is fuel, so you would be carrying an ignition source into more combustibles.
Cool a burning lithium pack with large volumes of water, never cover it, and never pick it up or carry it.
SAFO 09013, Fighting Fires Caused By Lithium Type Batteries in Portable Electronic Devices; SAFO 25002, Managing the Risks of Lithium Batteries (referenced for ACS UA.V.C.K2d)
https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/other_visit/aviation_industry/airline_operators/airline_safety/SAFO09013.pdf
Ice and blankets feel like cooling but insulate instead; water in volume is the cooling agent FAA guidance actually names.

UA.V.E.K5
You slept four hours, feel alert and have a deadline. What is the correct assessment?
Feeling alert proves you are fit enough to fly the job
Fatigue is not reliably self-detectable; do not fly
A strong coffee before launch resolves it
Fatigue degrades judgement before awareness. Subjective alertness is not evidence of fitness.
AIM 8-1-1(a)(5) Fitness for Flight - Fatigue; cf. 14 CFR 107.17

Wrong. The specific error is trusting self assessment. AIM 8-1-1, paragraph 5 (Fatigue), says fatigue "may not be apparent to a pilot until serious errors are made," so feeling alert is a sensation, not evidence, and it is exactly what fatigued pilots report before the mistake.

Correct. AIM 8-1-1 paragraph 5 treats fatigue as degrading performance and judgement before the pilot recognizes it, and 14 CFR 107.17 prohibits acting as remote PIC or VO when you know or have reason to know of a physical or mental condition that would interfere with safe operation. A four hour night is an objective deficit you can measure; alertness is not.

Wrong. Caffeine masks sleepiness without restoring the judgement and reaction time already lost, so it buys perceived alertness over real capability. AIM 8-1-1 paragraph 5 names adequate rest and sleep, plus regular exercise and proper nutrition, as the prevention; stimulants are not listed as a fix.
You cannot reliably self detect fatigue, so judge by hours of sleep rather than how you feel, and 107.17 grounds you when a condition would interfere with safe operation.
AIM 8-1-1, Fitness for Flight, paragraph 5 (Fatigue); 14 CFR 107.17
https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap8_section_1.html
Part 107 needs no medical certificate, but 107.17 still makes fitness a self grounding duty with real teeth.

UA.V.B.K3
An aircraft reports midfield left downwind for runway 31. Roughly what magnetic heading will it fly on final?

About 310 degrees magnetic. Runway 31 is aligned with a magnetic heading of about 310, and final approach is flown along the runway, so the aircraft heads about 310. On the left downwind it flies the reciprocal, about 130.
AIM 2-3-3(b) Runway Markings / Runway Designators

Correct. AIM 2-3-3(b) states the runway number is the whole number nearest one-tenth the magnetic azimuth of the runway centerline, so runway 31 points about 310 degrees magnetic, and an aircraft on final is lined up with that centerline.

Wrong. 130 is the reciprocal end (runway 13). This is the downwind-versus-final mix-up: a left downwind for runway 31 is actually flown on roughly 130, but the question asks for the heading on final, which is the opposite direction.

Wrong. This treats the painted designator as if it were already a three-digit heading. Read that way, 031 would belong to runway 3, not runway 31; designators are two digits and must be multiplied by 10.
Multiply the runway number by 10 to get its approximate magnetic heading, and that is the heading flown on final.
AIM 2-3-3(b), Runway Designators
https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap2_section_3.html

Any crew member assigned the task
The remote pilot in command

UA.III.B.K1c
The afternoon forecast calls for warm, moist, unstable air over your inspection site. What should you plan for?
Bumpy air, building cumulus and brief, heavy showers
Smooth air under a stratus deck with steady light drizzle
Calm wind and a haze layer that lingers all afternoon

Bumpy air, cumulus and showers. Unstable air keeps rising once lifted, so it builds cumuliform cloud with turbulence and showery precipitation, and visibility is usually good outside the showers. Smooth air, stratus, steady drizzle and trapped haze belong to stable air.
FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, p.26 (Stability of the Atmosphere table); also PHAK FAA-H-8083-25 p.12-12

Correct. The FAA stability table pairs unstable air with cumuliform clouds, showery precipitation, rough or turbulent air, and good visibility, because displaced air keeps rising on its own. Plan for gusts and a cell passing overhead.
Wrong. Smooth air, stratus and steady drizzle are the stable-air signature. They come from air that resists vertical motion, which is the opposite of the unstable air in the forecast.
Wrong. A lingering haze layer is what stable air does: with no vertical mixing, particulates stay concentrated near the surface. Unstable air mixes them upward and usually gives good visibility.
Unstable means rising air: cumulus clouds, showers, turbulence, and good visibility.
FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, p.26 (Stability of the Atmosphere)
https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/remote_pilot_study_guide.pdf
Good visibility belongs to unstable air, not stable air; rising currents scour the haze out.

UA.III.B.K1c
On a calm winter morning the briefer describes the air over your job site as stable. Which set of conditions fits that description?
Gusty air, towering cumulus, good visibility between showers
Smooth air, layered cloud, haze that holds visibility down
Smooth air, clear visibility and scattered afternoon showers

Smooth, layered and murky. Stable air resists vertical motion, so cloud spreads into stratiform layers, precipitation is steady rather than showery, and haze and smoke stay trapped near the surface, keeping visibility fair to poor.
FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, p.26 (Stability of the Atmosphere table)
Wrong. Every item here is unstable air: gusts and towering cumulus come from convection, and the good visibility between showers comes from vertical mixing that stable air does not have.
Correct. The FAA stability table lists stable air as stratiform clouds, steady or continuous precipitation such as drizzle, smooth air, and fair to poor visibility in haze and smoke.

Wrong. The smooth air is right, but clear visibility and showers both belong to unstable air. Showery precipitation needs convective lift and cumuliform cloud; stable air traps haze and gives steady precipitation instead.
Stable air is steady, stratiform, smooth, and murky; showery and cumuliform with clear air is unstable.
FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, p.26 (Stability of the Atmosphere)
https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/remote_pilot_study_guide.pdf
These distractors each get one half right; check the visibility word and the precipitation word separately.

UA.III.B.K1c
A low-level temperature inversion with high humidity produces what?
Smooth air, poor visibility, fog and haze
Rough air and good visibility as surface heat mixes upward
Thunderstorms as the warm layer aloft is forced upward

Smooth air with poor visibility in fog and haze. An inversion puts warm air over cool air, the most stable arrangement there is. It caps vertical mixing, so moisture, haze and smoke stay trapped in the cool layer below (PHAK Chapter 12).
PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 12 Weather Theory, p.12-13 (Temperature Inversion)

Correct. PHAK Chapter 12 (Temperature Inversion) states that an inversion aloft with high relative humidity in the cool air below produces smooth air with poor visibility from fog, haze, dust, and low stratus clouds.

Wrong. This reverses the stability. An inversion, warm air sitting on top of cool air, is the most stable arrangement there is, so it suppresses vertical motion rather than generating turbulence, and the trapped moisture ruins visibility rather than improving it.
Wrong. Thunderstorms need unstable air plus a lifting mechanism. An inversion acts as a lid that caps rising air, which is why it prevents convection instead of producing it.
Warm over cold is maximum stability: expect smooth air with fog, haze, and low stratus underneath.
PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 12, p.12-13 (Temperature Inversion)
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
The air inside the inversion is smooth, but wind shear often lurks right at the top of the layer.

UA.III.B.K1a
Effect of high density altitude on propeller efficiency?
Increased
Decreased
No effect

Decreased. High density altitude means thinner air, so each blade moves less air mass and makes less thrust, and engine power and rotor lift drop too (PHAK Chapter 11). Expect weaker climbs and a smaller payload margin on hot days.
PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 11 Aircraft Performance, p.11-2

Wrong. This comes from thinking thin air means less drag on the blades, so they must work better. A propeller is a rotating airfoil that produces thrust by accelerating a mass of air, so less dense air means less mass moved and less thrust.
Correct. PHAK Chapter 11 (Aircraft Performance) states that as density altitude increases, propeller efficiency decreases along with engine power and lift, because all three depend on air density.
Wrong. Saying density has no effect would mean thrust is independent of the air it works in. Density altitude degrades propeller thrust, engine power output, and wing or rotor lift together.
High density altitude means thin air, so the propeller has less mass to push and thrust falls off.
PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 11, p.11-2 (Density Altitude effects)
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
A propeller is a wing, not a fan blade cutting resistance; thinner air hurts it the same way it hurts lift.

UA.III.B.K1a
High density altitude results from what?
High temperature, high altitude, high humidity
Low temperature, low altitude, low humidity
High barometric pressure, cool air and dry conditions

Hot, high and humid. Density altitude rises with temperature, with elevation (lower pressure) and with humidity, because water vapor is lighter than dry air. Each makes the air thinner, cutting rotor lift and motor efficiency (PHAK Chapter 11).
PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 11 Aircraft Performance, p.11-5; identical wording in Remote Pilot Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22 p.21-22

Correct. PHAK Chapter 11 states that density altitude rises with increasing temperature, increasing altitude (decreasing pressure), and increasing humidity, since water vapor is lighter than dry air and displaces it.

Wrong. This lists every factor that makes air denser, so it describes LOW density altitude, the condition where the aircraft performs best. The three factors are correct but the direction is backwards.
Wrong. High pressure and cool air both increase air density, which lowers density altitude. This answer confuses high pressure the number with high density altitude the performance penalty.
Hot, high, and humid raises density altitude and degrades performance; cold, low, and dry lowers it.
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
High pressure gives low density altitude; the words high and low point in opposite directions here.

Magnetic north
True north
The active runway
True north in written reports. Winds given verbally by tower or ATIS are magnetic.

Correct. PHAK Chapter 13, METAR wind group, states that the wind direction in a coded METAR is given in degrees true north, in tens of degrees, followed by speed in knots.
Wrong. Wind relative to the runway is a headwind or crosswind component you calculate yourself. A METAR reports the ambient wind and knows nothing about which runway is active.
Written and coded weather (METAR, TAF) uses true north; winds spoken to you over the radio are magnetic.

A METAR reports OVC007. What does this mean?
Overcast at 700 ft
Overcast at 7,000 ft
Overcast at 70 ft
Overcast at 700 ft AGL. METAR cloud heights are three digits in hundreds of feet above the station, so 007 is 7 x 100 = 700 ft; 070 would be 7,000 ft. An overcast layer is also a ceiling.
PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 13 Aviation Weather Services, p.13-7 (Sky condition group); same wording in Remote Pilot Study Guide p.17
Correct. PHAK Chapter 13, sky condition group, states that cloud height is reported in hundreds of feet AGL using three digits, so 007 means 7 x 100 = 700 feet above the reporting station.
Wrong. This adds one zero too many, as if the digits were thousands of feet. The three-digit group is hundreds of feet, so 7,000 feet would be coded OVC070, not OVC007.
Wrong. This reads the group as tens of feet. Multiplying by 10 instead of 100 is the common arithmetic slip, and it would put an overcast deck below the 400 foot part 107 altitude limit.
Append two zeros to a METAR cloud group: three digits are hundreds of feet AGL above the station.

https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak

Which coverage codes constitute a ceiling?
FEW or SCT
BKN or OVC
CLR only

BKN or OVC. A ceiling is the height of the lowest layer reported as broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC), or the vertical visibility (VV) into an obscuration. FEW and SCT cover half the sky or less, so they never form a ceiling however low they sit.
PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 12 Weather Theory, p.12-17 (Ceiling)
Wrong. FEW (1/8 to 2/8) and SCT (3/8 to 4/8) cover less than half the sky, so they are not broken and never establish a ceiling no matter how low they sit.

Correct. PHAK Chapter 12 defines the ceiling as the height of the lowest layer of clouds reported as broken or overcast, or the vertical visibility into an obscuration, which requires coverage of 5/8 or more.
Wrong. CLR (or SKC) means no clouds reported, which is the absence of a ceiling, not a kind of ceiling. This answer reverses the definition entirely.
A ceiling is the lowest BKN, OVC, or vertical-visibility layer; FEW and SCT never count.
PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 12, p.12-17 (Ceiling)
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak

UA.III.B.K1i
Temperature 18 C, dewpoint 17 C. What does this suggest?
Fog or low cloud likely
Clear and dry air
Thunderstorms by afternoon

Fog or low cloud is likely. 18 C over a 17 C dewpoint is a 1 degree spread, so the air is almost saturated. Once the spread narrows to about 3 degrees or less, a little more cooling produces fog, mist or low stratus.
FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, p.25 (Moisture/Dew Point); PHAK p.12-14

Correct. The FAA study guide section on dewpoint explains that when temperature and dewpoint converge the air is near saturation, and a 1 C spread like this means fog, mist, or low stratus is likely, especially as the temperature falls toward the dewpoint.
Wrong. Clear and dry would require a wide temperature-dewpoint spread, which means the air must cool a long way before it saturates. A 1 C spread is the opposite condition.

Wrong. A narrow spread only tells you the air is nearly saturated. Thunderstorms additionally need an unstable lapse rate and a lifting mechanism, neither of which a temperature and dewpoint pair reveals.
When temperature and dewpoint are within about 2 C, expect fog, mist, or low cloud.
FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, p.25 (Moisture/Dew Point); PHAK p.12-14
https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/remote_pilot_study_guide.pdf

UA.III.B.K1e
Which thunderstorm stage features predominantly downdrafts?
Cumulus (developing)
Mature
Dissipating

Dissipating. The cumulus stage is mostly updrafts; the mature stage, which begins when rain reaches the ground, has updrafts and downdrafts side by side and is the most violent; the dissipating stage is predominantly downdrafts that choke off the warm inflow.
FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, p.28 (Thunderstorm life cycle); AC 00-24C para 4
Wrong. The cumulus (building) stage is defined by updrafts only; the FAA notes that precipitation has not yet begun to fall through the cell, which is exactly why there are no significant downdrafts.

Wrong. The mature stage has updrafts AND downdrafts side by side, which is what makes it the most violent stage. The question asks which stage is predominantly downdrafts, so having both disqualifies this one.
Correct. The FAA thunderstorm life cycle describes the dissipating stage as dominated by downdrafts, which cut off the warm, moist inflow the cell needs and starve it of energy.
Cumulus is updrafts, mature is both, dissipating is downdrafts.
FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, p.28 (Thunderstorm life cycle); AC 00-24C
https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/remote_pilot_study_guide.pdf

What is a microburst?
A brief intense downdraft producing severe wind shear
A small, short-lived thunderstorm cell under 2 miles wide
A burst of radio interference that can sever the control link
An intense localized downdraft. FAA figures: horizontal diameter 1 to 2 miles, depth about 1,000 ft, lifespan about 5 to 15 minutes, downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm, and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots.

Correct. The FAA study guide describes a microburst as a small, concentrated, intense downdraft about 1 to 2 miles across and roughly 1,000 feet deep, lasting about 5 to 15 minutes, with downdrafts to 6,000 fpm and horizontal wind changes of 30 to 90 knots.

Wrong. A microburst is a downdraft that occurs within or beneath a convective cell, not a cell itself. It has no cloud structure, life cycle, or lightning of its own, and one can hit under a rain shower or even under dry virga.
Wrong. This confuses the meteorological term with a radio-frequency burst. Microburst is strictly a wind shear phenomenon; nothing in FAA weather material uses it for electromagnetic interference.
A microburst is a concentrated downdraft, 1 to 2 miles wide, 5 to 15 minutes long, with 30 to 90 knots of wind shear.

https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/remote_pilot_study_guide.pdf

A forecast for the area around an airport
A routine hourly observation of current conditions
A chart supplement

Automated surface weather observing systems

Gradual change over many hours with widespread stratus
Rapid change, gusty wind, possible thunderstorms
No change

Added weight and disrupted airflow over props and airframe

When the operation is for aeronautical research or to show compliance with regulations and the FAA has authorized it
Whenever the flight remains below 200 ft AGL
Whenever the remote pilot files a flight plan

The remote ID rules carry a narrow exception for aeronautical research or showing compliance with regulations, and it requires FAA authorization. Otherwise no remote ID means flying only inside a FRIA.

Correct. 89.120 lets the Administrator authorize operation of an unmanned aircraft without remote identification when the operation is solely for aeronautical research or to show compliance with regulations, and 89.105 names it as an exception to the remote ID requirement. The FAA authorization is the operative part.

Wrong, because part 89 contains no altitude exception. The remote ID requirement applies from takeoff to shutdown regardless of height, and the 400 ft ceiling in 107.51(b) is an unrelated operating limit.

Wrong, because part 107 has no flight plan mechanism to file. Remote ID compliance comes only from a standard remote ID aircraft under 89.110, a broadcast module under 89.115(a), or staying inside a FRIA under 89.115(b).
No remote ID means FRIA only, unless the FAA has authorized the flight for aeronautical research or to show compliance with regulations.
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/subpart-B/section-89.120
Three self-service paths exist: standard remote ID, broadcast module, FRIA. The 89.120 research path requires FAA authorization, not your own say-so.

UA.I.F.K4
Does broadcasting ADS-B Out satisfy the remote identification requirement?
No, and part 107 separately prohibits operating with ADS-B Out in transmit mode unless authorized
Yes, ADS-B Out is an accepted alternative to remote ID
Yes, but only in controlled airspace

Two separate points. Remote ID is met by a standard remote ID aircraft, a broadcast module, or operating inside a FRIA. ADS-B Out is none of those, and 107.53 prohibits transmitting it without authorization.

Correct on both halves. Remote ID is satisfied only by 89.110, 89.115(a) or 89.115(b), none of which is ADS-B; and 107.53 prohibits operating a small unmanned aircraft system under part 107 with ADS-B Out equipment in transmit mode unless otherwise authorized by the Administrator, with 89.125 saying the same on the part 89 side.

Wrong, because 89.105 lists the accepted means and ADS-B is not among them. ADS-B Out is a surveillance system built for manned traffic and ATC displays, and for small UAS it is prohibited rather than accepted.

Wrong, because it inverts the logic. Controlled airspace is precisely where an unauthorized ADS-B Out transmission would clutter ATC and TCAS displays, and the 107.41 authorization governs airspace entry, never onboard equipment.
ADS-B Out never satisfies remote ID, and part 107 forbids transmitting it at all without FAA authorization.
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-B/section-107.53
107.52 does the same thing for transponders. Both are prohibitions, not equipment options.

UA.I.F.K5
Before takeoff, what must the remote PIC confirm about remote identification?
That the remote ID equipment is functioning and broadcasting, and it must broadcast from takeoff through shutdown
Only that the aircraft is registered
Nothing, the aircraft reports itself to the FAA automatically
Remote ID must broadcast from takeoff to shutdown. If you cannot confirm it is working before flight, the flight may not begin. If it fails in flight, end the flight as soon as practicable.

Correct. For a standard remote ID aircraft, 89.110(a)(1) requires broadcast of the 89.305 message elements from takeoff to shutdown and 89.110(b)(2) requires the equipment be functional and compliant across that whole period; for a broadcast module, 89.115(a)(3) requires a pre-flight check that the module is working and 89.115(a)(4), like 89.110(a)(2), requires landing as soon as practicable if the broadcast stops.

Wrong, because registration is a separate obligation under part 48. The serial number on the Certificate of Aircraft Registration matters to 89.110(b)(4), but a registration certificate tells you nothing about whether the broadcast is live right now.

Wrong, because remote ID is a local radio broadcast over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi that anyone nearby with a receiver can read. It is not telemetry uplinked to the FAA, and no agency system is listening for your aircraft on its own.
Confirm remote ID is broadcasting before takeoff, keep it broadcasting until shutdown, and land as soon as practicable if it quits.
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/subpart-B/section-89.110
Before takeoff a failure is a no-go; in flight it is land as soon as practicable, not land immediately.

UA.II.A.K4
What is air traffic control's primary function in the National Airspace System?
Preventing collisions and organizing the flow of traffic
Issuing and renewing pilot and remote pilot certificates
Enforcing aircraft registration requirements
Separation and traffic flow. ATC authorization for a part 107 flight in controlled airspace is about keeping you out of the way of manned traffic, not about approving your work.
FAA JO 7110.65, 2-1-1 ATC Service

Correct. FAA JO 7110.65, paragraph 2-1-1, states that the primary purpose of the ATC system is to prevent a collision involving aircraft operating in the system, along with providing a safe, orderly and expeditious flow of traffic.

Wrong, because certification is an airman certification function, not an ATC one. Remote pilot certificates are issued under part 107 subpart C, 107.63, through the FAA's certification process; no control facility has a role in it.

Wrong, because registration is administered under part 48 by the FAA Registry. Controllers do not police your paperwork, and an ATC authorization under 107.41 grants airspace access rather than blessing your registration or your operation.
ATC exists to prevent collisions and keep traffic flowing in an orderly, expeditious way, and nothing beyond that.
FAA JO 7110.65, paragraph 2-1-1 (ATC Service)

UA.II.B.K1
What are the basic weather minimums for a part 107 operation?
3 statute miles; 500 ft below and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds
1 statute mile and clear of clouds
3 nautical miles; 1,000 ft below and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds
3 SM, 500 below, 2,000 horizontal. Visibility is measured from the control station, not from the aircraft, and it is statute miles, not nautical.
14 CFR 107.51(c) and (d)

Correct. 107.51(c) sets minimum flight visibility at 3 statute miles as observed from the location of the control station, and 107.51(d) sets minimum cloud clearance at 500 ft below the cloud and 2,000 ft horizontally from the cloud.

Wrong because this is the manned day VFR minimum for Class G at or below 1,200 ft AGL under 91.155, borrowed from the wrong rulebook. Part 107 never permits a clear of clouds operation; there is always a 500 ft and 2,000 ft standoff.

Wrong on both numbers. Part 107 visibility is stated in statute miles, not nautical miles, and the vertical standoff is 500 ft below the cloud; the 1,000 ft below figure comes from the manned VFR cloud clearances in controlled airspace under 91.155.
Three, five hundred, two thousand: 3 statute miles visibility judged from the control station, 500 ft below clouds, 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds.
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-B/section-107.51
Visibility is measured from the control station, not from the aircraft, and it is statute, not nautical, miles.

UA.II.B.K3
You are operating in Class G airspace two miles from a non-towered airport. What does part 107 require?
Do not interfere with airport operations or traffic patterns
Nothing, because Class G carries no airport-related restriction
Written approval from the airport manager

107.43. No authorization is needed in Class G, but you may not interfere with airport operations or traffic patterns. Manned aircraft are lowest and slowest near airports, which is where your altitude band is.

Correct. 107.43 says no person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in a manner that interferes with operations and traffic patterns at any airport, heliport, or seaplane base, and that rule carries no airspace-class limit, so it applies in Class G exactly as it does in Class B.

Wrong because it confuses needing no ATC authorization with having no restriction. 107.41 is what exempts Class G from the authorization requirement; 107.43 is a separate, always-on prohibition that still binds you.

Wrong because no part 107 provision gives an airport manager authority to approve or deny your flight. Authorization, where it is required at all, comes from ATC through LAANC or DroneZone under 107.41, and only in controlled airspace.
107.41 decides whether you need authorization; 107.43 bans interference with airport traffic everywhere, Class G included.
14 CFR 107.43; see also 14 CFR 107.41
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-B/section-107.43

UA.II.B.K4c
Which of these should alert you that manned aircraft may be operating below 400 ft AGL?
Crop dusting, firefighting, or inspecting another aircraft in flight
Simply being in Class G airspace, where ATC does not separate traffic
Nighttime, when manned traffic shifts to low-level routes

These operations routinely bring manned aircraft into your altitude band. Emergency airborne inspection means one aircraft visually inspecting another in flight. See and avoid, and you are the one who yields.
AC 107-2A, 5.13 (See and Avoid / Right-of-Way) with 14 CFR 91.119(a), (c), (d)

Correct. Every operation listed has a working reason to be low: 91.119(c) and (d) let certain aircraft, including helicopters, operate below the usual minimum safe altitudes, and AC 107-2A paragraph 5.13 names these mission types as the ones that put manned traffic in your band. Under 107.37(a) you yield right of way to all of them.

Wrong because Class G is defined by the absence of ATC service, not by the altitude of the traffic in it. Low manned operations happen in every class of airspace, so the airspace letter by itself predicts nothing about a specific low-level mission.

Wrong because night changes your lighting and currency obligations under 107.29, not the kinds of missions flown near the ground. Medevac, law enforcement, and firefighting fly low day and night alike.
Any manned aircraft with a job to do near the ground, spraying, fire, police, banner, sling load, or in-flight inspection, can legally be in your 400 ft band, and you always yield.
https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/remote_pilot_study_guide.pdf
Right of way is one-directional: you give way, and the manned pilot is never required to see you first.

UA.II.B.K6
What should the remote pilot arrange at the control station for a night operation?
Dim lighting to read the controls without ruining night vision
Nothing, because the aircraft's own anti-collision lights are enough
Floodlights aimed at the aircraft throughout the flight
You still have to read your controller. Use lighting that lets you work while preserving dark adaptation, which takes roughly 30 minutes to build and seconds to lose.
AIM 8-1-6 Vision in Flight (dark adaptation); UAS ACS code UA.II.B.K6 'Operator equipment for night flight'

Correct. ACS code UA.II.B.K6 covers operator equipment for night flight, and AIM 8-1-6 explains that full dark adaptation takes at least 30 minutes while a usable degree can be held under dim lighting, so the station needs just enough light to read the controller without washing out your eyes.

Wrong because it mixes up the two lighting jobs. The anti-collision lighting required by 107.29(a)(2) exists so other people can see the aircraft; it does nothing to let you read your own display, battery state, or checklist.

Wrong because floodlighting the aircraft destroys the dark adaptation you need to keep it in visual line of sight under 107.31, and can distract or blind others on the ground. The regulation puts lighting on the aircraft, not on the ground pointed at it.
Light the control station only enough to read it, and keep bright white light out of your own eyes: 30 minutes to build night vision, seconds to lose it.
AIM 8-1-6 Vision in Flight; ACS UA.II.B.K6; contrast 14 CFR 107.29(a)(2)
https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap8_section_1.html
Aircraft lighting is so others see you; control station lighting is so you can see your gear. Different problems, different fixes.

UA.II.B.K7
Why survey a night operating site during daylight first?
Towers, wires and antennas are far harder to see at night
Because night operations require a daytime site authorization
Because GPS accuracy degrades noticeably after dark
Wires are close to invisible at night and often hard to see in daylight. Survey while you can see, and note every obstacle and its position relative to your launch point.
14 CFR 107.49(a); FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide, VFR chapter, OBSTRUCTIONS; AC 70/7460-1N para. Application; ACS UA.II.B.K7 "Ground structures and ground structure lighting"

Correct. 107.49(a)(4) makes other ground hazards part of your mandatory preflight assessment, and AC 70/7460-1N recommends marking and lighting only for certain structures, so many towers, guy wires, and antennas are legally unlit. Daylight is when you can actually find them and fix their position relative to your launch point.

Wrong because no such thing as a daytime authorization exists. Since the 2021 amendment, night operation under 107.29(a) needs only current knowledge testing or recurrent training plus the required anti-collision lighting, with no waiver and no separate approval.

Wrong because GNSS performance has nothing to do with daylight; the satellites are in the same orbits at midnight. The night hazard is your inability to see obstacles, not a degraded position solution.
Preflight the site while you can still see it: 107.49(a)(4) makes ground hazards your responsibility, and unlit wires and towers are the ones that bite after dark.
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-B/section-107.49
Night flight needs no waiver since April 2021. It needs anti-collision lighting, current training, and a site you already walked.

UA.II.B.K8
An obstruction near your night operating site is neither lit nor charted. What does that mean for you?
Charts and lights are incomplete; clearance is still on you
If it is not charted, it is not a hazard you need to plan around
You may assume it is below 200 ft AGL, the charting cutoff
Charts show obstacles above certain heights and lighting requirements do not reach every structure. Your own site survey is the authority, not the chart.
FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide, VFR chapter, OBSTRUCTIONS; AC 70/7460-1N, Application; 14 CFR 107.49(a)(4)

Correct. 107.49(a)(4) puts other ground hazards on the remote PIC regardless of what any publication shows. The Chart User's Guide explains that VFR charts depict obstructions by selective criteria, and AC 70/7460-1N applies marking and lighting recommendations only to certain structures, so neither is a complete inventory.

Wrong because it treats the sectional as an exhaustive hazard database. Charts omit obstructions below the charting thresholds, newly built structures may not be charted yet, and nothing in part 107 makes chart depiction the test of whether something can be hit.

Wrong because it invents an altitude guarantee that no rule provides. Charting and lighting thresholds are reporting criteria, not a promise about any particular uncharted object, and your clearance duty under 107.49(a)(4) is unchanged either way.
Charts and obstruction lights are incomplete by design; your own site survey, not the chart, is the authority on what is out there.
14 CFR 107.49(a)(4); FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide, VFR section, Obstructions; AC 70/7460-1N

UA.II.B.K9
During a night survey you see another aircraft crossing your view showing a single steady green light and no red light. Which way is it moving?
From your right to your left
From your left to your right
Directly toward you

From your left to your right. Position lights are red on the aircraft's left wingtip, green on its right. Seeing only green means its right side faces you, which happens when it crosses from your left to your right. Only red would mean right to left; red and green together mean nose-on.
FAA Airplane Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-3C, Chapter 11, Night Operations (Airplane Lighting); ACS UA.II.B.K9 "Manned aircraft lighting"
Wrong because an aircraft crossing from your right to your left shows you its left side, so you would see only the red left-wingtip light, not the green one.

Correct. Position lights are red on the aircraft's left wingtip and green on its right, per the Airplane Flying Handbook night operations discussion. A crossing aircraft that shows only green has its right side toward you, so it is moving from your left to your right. You still give way under 107.37(a).
Wrong because an aircraft heading straight at you shows both wingtips at once, red on your right and green on your left. A single color means you are seeing it side-on, not nose-on.
Red left, green right on the aircraft. One color means it is crossing: green only, left to right; red only, right to left. Both colors means nose-on.
FAA Airplane Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-3C, Ch. 11 Night Operations (Airplane Lighting); ACS UA.II.B.K9; see also 14 CFR 107.37(a)
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/airplane_handbook
Both colors at once equals head-on. One color equals crossing. Red and green swapped equals going away.

UA.II.B.K10
What lighting must a small unmanned aircraft carry for night operations?
Flashing anti-collision lights visible for 3 statute miles
A steady white light visible for at least 1 statute mile
Red and green navigation lights only, like a manned aircraft
3 statute miles, flashing. Steady lights do not satisfy the rule. The remote PIC may reduce intensity only where operating conditions make that the safer choice.
14 CFR 107.29(a)(2); ACS UA.II.B.K10 "sUAS lighting requirements"

Correct. 107.29(a)(2) requires lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles with a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision, and 107.29(b) imposes the identical requirement during civil twilight. The remote PIC may reduce the intensity in the interest of safety but may never extinguish it.

Wrong on two counts. A steady light cannot satisfy a requirement written as a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision, and 1 statute mile appears nowhere in 107.29; the visibility figure in the rule is 3 statute miles.

Wrong because red and green position lights are a manned aircraft requirement under 91.209 and are not what 107.29(a)(2) asks for. Nav lights help determine an aircraft's direction of flight; they are not anti-collision lighting and do not meet the part 107 standard on their own.
Night and civil twilight both demand anti-collision lighting visible 3 statute miles and flashing; dim it for safety if you must, never switch it off.
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-B/section-107.29

UA.III.A.K1
Which is an official source of aviation weather for preflight planning?
Flight Service (1800wxbrief.com) or aviationweather.gov
A consumer smartphone weather app with live radar overlays
A local television station's hourly forecast
Use aviation weather sources. Consumer forecasts do not give you METARs, TAFs, ceilings, density altitude, or AIRMET and SIGMET information.
AIM para 7-1-2 FAA Weather Services and 7-1-3 Use of Aviation Weather Products; Remote Pilot Study Guide p.14

Correct. AIM 7-1-2 identifies FAA and National Weather Service products and outlets, Flight Service and the Aviation Weather Center among them, as the sources for flight planning, and 107.49(a)(1) makes assessing local weather conditions a required preflight action.

Wrong because consumer apps are not FAA-approved weather sources. AIM 7-1-3 cautions against relying on non-approved products, and a consumer app will not give you METARs, TAFs, AIRMETs, SIGMETs, ceilings in AGL, or density altitude.

Wrong because a television forecast is a public-interest product aimed at the general population, not an aviation observation or forecast. It carries no station observations, no cloud layer coding, and no convective or icing advisories you can plan a flight against.
Preflight weather comes from an FAA or NWS aviation source, and 107.49(a)(1) makes checking local weather a required preflight action, not an option.
https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap7_section_1.html

UA.III.A.K4
What does a surface analysis chart give you that a METAR does not?
Fronts and pressure systems across a wide area
The exact cloud height over your launch point right now
Airspace class boundaries
Charts give you the big picture and the trend. A METAR gives you a point observation. You need both: the METAR tells you now, the chart tells you what is coming.
PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 13 Aviation Weather Services, p.13-13 (Surface Analysis Chart)

Correct. PHAK Chapter 13 describes the surface analysis chart as a depiction of fronts, high and low pressure centers, and station observations over a broad area, which is exactly the synoptic trend information a single-station report cannot supply.

Wrong because that is precisely the METAR's job, not the chart's. A surface analysis is a wide-area snapshot built from many stations; it does not resolve the cloud base over one launch point at one moment.
Wrong because it confuses a weather chart with an aeronautical chart. Airspace class boundaries live on VFR sectionals and terminal area charts; no weather product depicts them.
The METAR tells you what is happening here now; the surface analysis chart tells you what is moving toward here.
PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Ch. 13 Aviation Weather Services (Surface Analysis Chart)

UA.III.B.K1b
You are flying on the downwind side of a large building in a 15 knot wind. What should you expect?
Mechanical turbulence and strong sinking air
Smoother air sheltered from the wind than on the upwind side
No measurable effect below 400 ft AGL
Wind striking an obstruction breaks into mechanical turbulence and rolls downward on the lee side. Small aircraft are easily overpowered by it. Plan to approach obstacles from upwind.
PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 12 Weather Theory, p.12-9 to 12-10 (Effect of Obstructions on Wind); same wording in Remote Pilot Study Guide p.23

Correct. PHAK Chapter 12, Effect of Obstructions on Wind, describes wind striking a building or terrain feature breaking into eddies with strong downdrafts on the lee side. A small unmanned aircraft has little excess power, so that sink can exceed its climb capability, which is why 107.49(a)(1) makes local weather a preflight item.
Wrong because the lee side is the rough side, not the sheltered one. Flow upwind of the obstruction is comparatively undisturbed; it is downwind that it tumbles into eddies and rotors.

Wrong because mechanical turbulence is worst near the surface, which is the entire band part 107 confines you to under 107.51(b). Low altitude is where obstruction effects are strongest, not where they disappear.
Wind hitting an obstruction tumbles and sinks on the downwind side, so approach buildings and tree lines from upwind.
PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Ch. 12 Weather Theory (Effect of Obstructions on Wind); 14 CFR 107.49(a)(1)
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak

UA.III.B.K1f
A tornado is reported near your operating area. What is the correct response?
Do not fly; the storm's hazards reach far beyond the funnel
Fly, but stay below 100 ft AGL where friction slows the wind
Fly, staying upwind of the funnel and at least 5 miles from it
A tornado indicates an intense thunderstorm and the hazard extends far beyond what you can see. This is a do not fly condition, not a distance to be managed.
AC 00-24C Thunderstorms, para 7.a(2) and 7.a(3)

Correct. AC 00-24C paragraph 7.a treats a tornado as evidence of an extremely intense thunderstorm, with violent wind and turbulence extending far outside the visible funnel. Combined with the 107.19(c) duty not to create an undue hazard and the 107.49(a)(1) weather assessment, the only defensible answer is to cancel.

Wrong because altitude is not a mitigation here. The low-level band is where the gust front, outflow winds, and airborne debris are most severe, so flying lower moves you toward the hazard, not away from it.

Wrong because thunderstorm guidance is avoidance, not offsetting. A tornado and its parent cell move and redevelop, your upwind position can become downwind within minutes, and the damaging wind field extends well beyond anything you can see.
A tornado report is a cancelled flight, not a distance to be managed.
AC 00-24C para 7.a; 14 CFR 107.19(c); 14 CFR 107.49(a)(1); PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Ch. 12 (Tornadoes)
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak

UA.III.B.K1h
Where can hail be encountered relative to a thunderstorm?
Well outside the storm, even in clear air miles away
Only directly beneath the cloud base, inside the rain shaft
Only above the freezing level inside the cloud
Hail can be thrown from the top of a cell and carried miles downwind, falling through clear air. Distance from the visible cloud is not the same as safety.
AC 00-24C Thunderstorms, para 7.d(1)

Correct. AC 00-24C paragraph 7.d explains that hail can be thrown out of the storm top by the updraft and carried downwind, so it falls through apparently clear air miles from the visible cloud. PHAK Chapter 12 makes the same point about clear-air hail.

Wrong because hail forms above the freezing level but does not stay there. It grows by cycling in the updraft, then falls out of the cell and can be flung well away from it laterally.
Hail can fall out of clear air miles from the cell, so the edge of the visible cloud is not the edge of the hazard.
AC 00-24C para 7.d; PHAK FAA-H-8083-25, Ch. 12 Weather Theory (Hail)

UA.III.B.K1j
What is a ceiling?
Height of the lowest BKN or OVC layer, or vertical visibility
The height above ground of the highest reported cloud layer
The highest altitude you are permitted to fly in that airspace

Wrong because it confuses a weather observation with a regulatory limit. Your maximum altitude is the 400 ft AGL figure in 107.51(b); the ceiling is simply a reported cloud height and is not itself a flight restriction.
Ceiling equals the lowest BKN or OVC layer, reported in hundreds of feet AGL; FEW and SCT never count.

UA.III.B.K1k
You see lightning in the distance during a planned operation. What does that tell you?
A thunderstorm is near; its gust front can beat the rain
Nothing yet, unless rain or hail is already falling at your site
That the storm is dissipating and conditions are improving
Lightning means a thunderstorm, and a thunderstorm's gust front can arrive well ahead of the cell itself. Land and secure the aircraft rather than trying to finish the flight.
FAA Aviation Weather Handbook FAA-H-8083-28, Ch. 22 Thunderstorms; corroborated by AC 00-24C, Thunderstorms

Correct. Lightning is the defining evidence of a thunderstorm, and the Aviation Weather Handbook Chapter 22 and AC 00-24C both describe the gust front and outflow arriving well ahead of the cell. Wrong because rain at your site is not the trigger for action. The gust front, strong downdrafts, and wind shear precede the precipitation, so waiting for rain means waiting until the hazard is already on top of you.
Wrong because lightning indicates an active or developing convective cell, which is deterioration, not improvement. Nothing about a visible discharge suggests the situation is getting better.
Distant lightning means land now; the gust front gets to you before the rain does.

UA.V.A.K1
What is the practical difference between a towered and a non-towered airport?
At a towered airport ATC sequences traffic; at a non-towered airport pilots self-announce on a common frequency and separate themselves
A non-towered airport has no traffic pattern
A towered airport requires no ATC authorization for part 107 operations

Remove it from service and dispose of it per the manufacturer's instructions; do not fly it and do not charge it
Fly it until it no longer holds a charge, then discard it
Puncture it to relieve the internal pressure
Swelling indicates internal damage. A damaged lithium cell can enter thermal runaway, which is self-sustaining and burns intensely. Never puncture a pack and never charge a damaged one.
14 CFR 107.15(a) and (b)

Correct. 14 CFR 107.15(a) makes the remote pilot in command responsible for determining the small unmanned aircraft system is in a condition for safe operation before flight, and inspecting it to that standard. Slightly off to one side of it, because the center of vision is nearly blind in low light
Directly at it, holding your gaze steady

None of Categories 1, 2 or 3. Exposed rotating parts that would lacerate human skin disqualify an aircraft from Categories 1, 2 and 3 (107.110(a)(2), 107.120(a)(2), 107.130(a)(2)). Props that cannot lacerate skin would not disqualify it (see the related Category 1 item). Weight alone never makes an aircraft eligible, and at 0.9 lb it independently exceeds the 0.55 lb Category 1 limit. Category 4 is a separate path requiring a part 21 airworthiness certificate and approved Flight Manual limitations, not a weight or rotating-parts test.

Correct. The identical no-exposed-rotating-parts clause appears in 107.110(a)(2) for Category 1, 107.120(a)(2) for Category 2 and 107.130(a)(2) for Category 3: the aircraft must not contain any exposed rotating parts that would lacerate human skin upon impact with a human being. Bare props fail all three, and 107.110(a)(1) separately caps Category 1 at 0.55 lb on takeoff and throughout the flight including everything attached, so 0.9 lb fails Category 1 twice over.

Wrong. This treats Category 1 as a pure weight class. Category 1 has two tests in 107.110(a), weight AND no exposed lacerating rotating parts, and this aircraft misses both: 0.9 lb is well over the 0.55 lb limit and the props are bare.

Wrong. 55 lb is the part 107 definition of a small unmanned aircraft under 107.3, not a Category 3 criterion. Category 3 eligibility in 107.130(a) is a 25 ft-lb kinetic-energy-transfer limit plus the same no-exposed-rotating-parts clause, so being under 55 lb is simply the price of admission to part 107 at all.
Exposed rotating parts that could lacerate skin bar an aircraft from Categories 1, 2 and 3 regardless of how little it weighs.

UA.I.C.K1
You refuse a test for drugs or alcohol requested in connection with an operation. What may follow?
Denial of an application for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation of your certificate
Nothing, refusal is your right
A civil penalty only, with no effect on the certificate
107.59 makes refusal itself grounds for denial for up to one year and for suspension or revocation.

Correct. 14 CFR 107.59 states that refusing a blood alcohol test requested by a law enforcement officer under 91.17(c), or refusing to furnish or authorize release of results requested by the Administrator under 91.17(c) or (d), is grounds for (a) denial of an application for a remote pilot certificate with a small UAS rating for up to 1 year after the refusal, or (b) suspension or revocation of that certificate.

Wrong. This reads a constitutional criminal-procedure instinct into an administrative certificate rule. You may decline the officer, but 107.59 makes the refusal itself an independent ground for FAA certificate action, so the consequence attaches whether or not any test result ever exists.

Wrong. 107.59 is specifically a certificate-action section: both of its listed consequences are certificate consequences (denial for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation). A civil penalty may also be available under other authority, but saying there is no effect on the certificate directly contradicts the text.
Refusing an alcohol test, or refusing to release the results, is itself grounds for denial of an application for up to 1 year or suspension or revocation of your certificate.
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-C/section-107.59

UA.II.B.K9
At night another aircraft shows you a red light on your left and a green light on your right. What is it doing?
Flying away from you
Flying toward you
Hovering in place
Red is the aircraft's left wingtip, green its right. Seeing red on your left means you are looking at the aircraft's left wing from behind, so it is heading away.
FAA Airplane Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-3C, Chapter 11, Night Operations (Airplane Lighting); ACS UA.II.B.K9 "Manned aircraft lighting"

Correct. Position lights are fixed to the airframe: red on the aircraft's left wingtip, green on its right, white at the tail. If the red light appears on YOUR left and green on YOUR right, the aircraft's left and right agree with yours, which only happens when you are looking at its tail, so it is going away from you.

Wrong. This is the single most common position-light error: forgetting that facing an aircraft mirrors its left and right. An aircraft coming at you shows its red left wingtip on YOUR right and its green right wingtip on YOUR left, the reverse of what is described.

Wrong. Position lights encode the aircraft's orientation, not its speed, so they cannot report a hover; and the red/green arrangement given is specifically a tail-on view. Treat this as a geometry question: match the colors to sides and read off which way the nose points.
Red is the left wingtip and green the right, so red-on-your-left means you are behind it and it is going away; green-on-your-left means it is coming at you.
AIM 4-3-24 (Use of Aircraft Lights); 14 CFR 91.209; FAA Airplane Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-3C Ch. 11 (Night Operations)
https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap4_section_3.html
The colors are on the AIRCRAFT's left and right, so a head-on view swaps which side you see them on.

UA.II.B.K3
You are one mile from a non-towered airport in Class G at 200 ft AGL when you hear an aircraft announce a three mile final. What is correct?
Move clear of the final approach path or land
Continue, because Class G imposes no requirement
Climb to 400 ft AGL so the pilot can see you
107.43. Not interfering is an active obligation. Climbing puts you closer to the traffic, not further from it.
14 CFR 107.43; 14 CFR 107.41 (no ATC authorization needed in Class G); ACS UA.II.B.K3 "Operations near airports"

Correct. 14 CFR 107.43 bars operating in a manner that interferes with operations and traffic patterns at any airport, heliport or seaplane base, and 107.37(a) requires you to yield the right of way to all aircraft. Both duties are active: hearing the call means you move out of the approach path or land, without waiting to be asked.

Wrong. Class G means no ATC authorization is required under 107.41, and students routinely over-read that as no obligation at all. 107.43 and 107.37(a) apply in every class of airspace, towered or not, and neither one is even waivable for Class G.

Wrong. This inverts the right-of-way rule, trading separation for visibility. Climbing to 400 ft moves you up into the arriving aircraft's descent path on a three mile final, and being seen is not a defense under 107.37(a), which puts the duty to yield on you, not on the manned pilot.
107.43 applies in every class of airspace: get out of the way of airport traffic, do not climb up to be noticed.
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-B/section-107.43

UA.III.B.K1j
A METAR reports SCT015 BKN030 OVC080. What is the ceiling?
The ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer. SCT015 is scattered and does not count, so BKN030, meaning 3,000 ft, is the ceiling.
FAA Remote Pilot - sUAS Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), Ch. 3a: ceiling definition plus sky cover table (FEW 1/8-2/8, SCT 3/8-4/8, BKN 5/8-7/8, OVC 8/8) and height convention

Correct. The ceiling is the height of the lowest BROKEN or OVERCAST layer, or the vertical visibility into an obscuration. Heights in a METAR are in hundreds of feet above ground level, so BKN030 is 3,000 ft AGL and it is the lowest layer reported as BKN or OVC.

Wrong. SCT015 is 1,500 ft, but SCT means 3/8 to 4/8 sky cover, which is not enough to constitute a ceiling. The misconception is reading the lowest reported layer as the ceiling instead of the lowest qualifying layer; FEW (1/8 to 2/8) and SCT never count.

Wrong. OVC080 is 8,000 ft and does qualify as a ceiling layer, but the definition says LOWEST, not most solid. Students pick this because 8/8 overcast feels more ceiling-like; once BKN030 exists below it, the higher overcast is irrelevant.
Ceiling is the LOWEST layer reported BKN or OVC (or vertical visibility), read in hundreds of feet AGL; FEW and SCT never count.
FAA-G-8082-22 Remote Pilot - sUAS Study Guide, Ch. 3 (METAR sky condition and ceiling); FAA-H-8083-28 Aviation Weather Handbook (sky cover: FEW 1/8-2/8, SCT 3/8-4/8, BKN 5/8-7/8, OVC 8/8)
https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/remote_pilot_study_guide.pdf
Lowest broken or overcast, not thickest; and the digits are hundreds of feet AGL, not feet MSL.

UA.III.B.K1h
A thunderstorm cell sits eight miles from your site and the sky overhead is clear. Which hazard can still reach you?
Hail thrown from the cell's top, and its gust front
None, because storms only threaten within about 5 miles
Only reduced visibility from dust raised well ahead of the cell
Hail is carried well downwind and gust fronts run out ahead of the cell. Clear sky overhead is not clearance.
FAA AC 00-24C, Thunderstorms; corroborated by FAA Aviation Weather Handbook FAA-H-8083-28, Ch. 22

Correct. FAA weather guidance is explicit that hail can be thrown out of the anvil top and fall in clear air several miles from the cell, and that the gust front of cold outflow can precede the storm by 15 miles or more with low-level wind shear and sharp wind shifts. That is why the FAA's avoidance standard is 20 miles from a thunderstorm, which 8 miles does not satisfy.

Wrong. This equates a clear sky overhead with safety. Both of the hazards that reach farthest from a cell, hail in the anvil and the outflow gust front, specifically arrive under clear air ahead of the storm, which is exactly why the 20-mile rule is stated as a distance rather than as a what-you-can-see test.

Wrong. Blowing dust is a visible symptom of the gust front, not the hazard itself. The gust front brings a sudden wind-speed and direction change that will exceed a small UAS's wind capability and can flip or push it out of VLOS, and hail is in play too, so limiting the answer to visibility badly understates it.
Stay 20 miles from a thunderstorm: hail from the anvil and the gust front both reach far ahead of the cell into clear air.
FAA AC 00-24C (Thunderstorms); FAA-H-8083-28 Aviation Weather Handbook, Ch. 22 (Thunderstorms); FAA-H-8083-25 PHAK Ch. 12 (20-mile avoidance)
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Clear sky overhead is not clearance; the number to remember is 20 miles.

UA.V.E.K6
You look directly at a distant object at night and it disappears. Why?
The center of your vision has few rods and is nearly blind in low light, so off-center viewing is needed
Your eyes have not yet adjusted to the controller screen
The object moved out of your field of view
This is the night blind spot. Scan slightly to the side of what you want to see.
FAA Pilot Vision brochure (CAMI) / Airplane Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-3C Ch.11

Correct. The center of the retina (the fovea) is packed with cones, which need daylight-level illumination, and has almost no rods. Rods handle low light and sit off-center, so a dim object you center in your vision lands on the night blind spot and vanishes. The fix is off-center viewing: look about 10 degrees to the side and scan in short, deliberate steps.

Wrong. Losing dark adaptation to a bright controller screen is a real night hazard, but it dims everything in the scene and takes 20 to 30 minutes to recover. It does not make one centered object disappear and then reappear the moment you glance slightly off to the side.

Wrong. The object is disproved by the test itself: look a little to one side and it comes back, so nothing moved. What changed is which part of your retina the image fell on, not the geometry of the scene.
Cones sit in the center and need light; rods sit off-center, so at night look about 10 degrees to the side of what you want to see.
FAA Pilot Vision brochure (FAA Civil Aerospace Medical Institute); FAA-H-8083-25 PHAK Ch. 17 (Aeromedical Factors, vision in flight); FAA-H-8083-3C Airplane Flying Handbook Ch. 11
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
The night blind spot (center of vision) and dark adaptation (20 to 30 minutes) are two different problems.

UA.V.B.K8
An airport rotating beacon is operating at ten in the morning in Class D airspace. What does that suggest?
Weather at the field may be below basic VFR minimums
The control tower is closed
The airport is a military field
In Class D a beacon running in daylight commonly indicates the field is IFR. Note that it does not change your part 107 minimums, which remain 3 statute miles and 500 below, 2,000 horizontal.
AIM 2-1-9(b) Airport/Heliport Beacons; 14 CFR 107.51(c)-(d)

Correct. AIM 2-1-9 states that in Class B, C, D and E surface areas, operation of the airport beacon during daylight hours often indicates the ground visibility is less than 3 miles and/or the ceiling is less than 1,000 ft, that is, IFR conditions. The AIM also warns that a beacon is not a guarantee either way, which is why the answer is worded may be.

Wrong. A closed tower is announced by NOTAM and shows up as the surface airspace reverting to Class E or G, not by the beacon. Beacons run every night with the tower fully staffed, so beacon operation carries no information about tower status.

Wrong. Military fields are identified by the beacon's flash PATTERN, not by when it runs: AIM 2-1-9 describes military airport beacons as flashing alternating white and green with two quick white flashes between the green. Time of day tells you about weather, not about who owns the field.
A rotating beacon running in daylight at a surface-area airport means the field is probably IFR; it says nothing about tower hours or who owns the airport.
AIM 2-1-9 (Airport/Heliport Beacons), paragraphs 3 and 4; 14 CFR 107.51(c) and (d)
https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap2_section_1.html
A daytime beacon is a weather hint only, and it does not relax your part 107 minimums of 3 SM visibility and 500 below / 2,000 horizontal from clouds.

UA.V.C.K2b
Which practice reduces lithium battery fire risk?
Charge on a non-combustible surface, never unattended, and never charge a swollen or damaged pack
Charge at the highest available current to shorten charge time
Store packs fully charged in a hot vehicle

Lithium-polymer fires start from heat, physical damage, and overcharge. Charging on a non-combustible surface contains a failure, staying with the pack lets you intervene early, and a swollen or crash-damaged cell is already compromised and must never be recharged. Charging at the highest available current adds heat and thermal-runaway risk, and storing a fully charged pack in a hot vehicle combines the two worst stressors.

FAA-S-ACS-10B (Remote Pilot sUAS ACS, eff. April 6, 2021), Area V, Task C, UA.V.C.K2b/K2c; MTSU Remote Pilot sUAS Knowledge Test Study Guide, Task C. Emergency Procedures (lithium battery section). FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22) and AC 107-2A contain no lithium-battery charging text.

Correct. All three halves of this answer attack the known triggers of lithium-polymer thermal runaway, which the ACS tests under UA.V.C.K2b as a battery hazard and emergency-procedure item: a non-combustible surface contains a venting pack, attended charging lets you pull the plug at the first sign of heat or swelling, and a puffed or crash-damaged cell has already failed internally and must be retired rather than recharged.

Wrong. This treats charge current as a convenience setting. Charge rate is a heat source, and heat is the primary driver of thermal runaway, so exceeding the manufacturer's specified charge rate raises the exact risk the question asks you to reduce.

Wrong. This stacks the two worst stressors. Lithium packs should be stored at a partial charge per the manufacturer, not fully charged, and a parked vehicle's interior reaches temperatures far above any safe storage range; full state of charge plus high temperature is a textbook thermal-runaway setup.
Non-combustible surface, never unattended, the manufacturer's charge rate, and never recharge a swollen or crash-damaged pack.
FAA-S-ACS-10B Remote Pilot sUAS ACS (eff. April 6, 2021), Area V, Task C, UA.V.C.K2b/K2c (battery hazards and emergency procedures); FAA Office of Hazardous Materials Safety lithium battery guidance
https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/remote_pilot_study_guide.pdf
A swollen pack is not usable at reduced capacity; it is retired. Also note no part 107 regulation covers charging, so this is an ACS/manufacturer item, not a CFR one.

UA.V.D.K1b
During a complex operation your workload spikes at the worst moment. What does task management ask you to do?
Plan and prioritize tasks ahead, then shed low-priority ones
Delegate the preflight inspection to a visual observer
Work faster so that every task on the checklist still gets done

Workload, planned in advance. Task saturation and channelized attention are how a remote pilot loses situational awareness. Sequence the tasks before you launch, brief the crew on who does what, and when workload spikes drop the things that can wait rather than trying to do everything at once.
FAA-H-8083-25 PHAK Ch. 2 (task management); ACS UA.V.D.K1b

Correct. Task management as the FAA defines it has two halves: sequence and prioritize the flight's tasks before you launch, and when workload rises, recognize the saturation and shed the low-priority items so capacity goes to flying the aircraft and keeping it in sight. This is the ACS Area V, Task D single-pilot resource management content and PHAK Ch. 2 on task management.

Wrong. The preflight check is not delegable. 14 CFR 107.15(a) puts the duty on the remote pilot in command to check the sUAS before each flight, and 107.19 makes the remote PIC directly responsible for the operation; a visual observer's job is seeing and avoiding, not certifying the aircraft.

Wrong. Speeding up is what task saturation already makes you do, and it produces skipped checks, channelized attention and loss of situational awareness. The remedy in FAA human-factors material is to drop tasks, not to accelerate through all of them.
Task management means prioritizing the flight's tasks before launch, then shedding the low-priority ones when workload spikes.

FAA-S-ACS-10B Remote Pilot sUAS ACS, Area V, Task D (UA.V.D.K1b, task management); FAA-H-8083-25 PHAK Ch. 2 (Aeronautical Decision-Making, task management and situational awareness); 14 CFR 107.15(a), 107.19
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
The remote PIC owns the preflight check under 107.15(a); a visual observer is never a place to dump workload.

UA.II.B.K4a
What is the leading causal factor in aviation accidents?
Human error, including poor decision making
Mechanical failure of the airframe or propulsion system
Unforecast weather such as sudden gusts or low cloud

Human error. FAA training material consistently treats human factors, such as poor decision making and loss of situational awareness, not mechanical failure, as the leading contributor to accidents. That is why aeronautical decision making, crew resource management and the five hazardous attitudes are tested at all.
FAA-H-8083-25 PHAK Ch. 2 (Aeronautical Decision-Making); FAA-G-8082-22

Correct. PHAK Ch. 2 states that human error is the cause or a contributing factor in the large majority of aviation accidents, which is exactly why the FAA builds an entire test area around aeronautical decision-making, crew resource management, the five hazardous attitudes and their antidotes, and situational awareness.

Wrong. Airframe and equipment failures do cause accidents, but they are the minority; decades of FAA and NTSB accident data put the pilot, not the machine, at the top. Picking this also fails to explain why the ACS devotes a whole area to human factors rather than to maintenance.

Wrong. Weather shows up in a great many accidents, but in FAA analysis it usually lands under human error: the decision to launch into it, or the decision to press on once conditions deteriorated. The hazard was present; the causal factor was the choice.
Human error, not hardware and not the weather itself, is behind most aviation accidents, which is why ADM is a tested area.
FAA-H-8083-25 PHAK Ch. 2 (Aeronautical Decision-Making); FAA-G-8082-22 Remote Pilot Study Guide (Crew Resource Management / ADM section); AC 107-2A Ch. 5
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Weather-related accidents usually count as human error, because the causal factor is the decision to launch or to continue.

UA.III.B.K1d
What are characteristics of a moist, unstable air mass?
Turbulence and showery precipitation.
Poor visibility and smooth air.
Haze and smoke.

Unstable air lets a parcel keep rising once displaced, so moisture builds cumuliform clouds, which produce vertical currents (turbulence) and showery, intermittent rain. Poor visibility with smooth air is the signature of a STABLE moist air mass (stratus, fog, drizzle), and haze and smoke are stable-air traits too because stagnant air traps pollutants. The trap is that both wrong options are real air-mass descriptions, just for stable air.
FAA-H-8083-25 Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Ch. 12 (Weather Theory), atmospheric stability; FAA-G-8082-22 Remote Pilot Study Guide, weather section

Correct. In unstable air a displaced parcel keeps rising on its own, so moisture builds CUMULIFORM clouds. The vertical currents inside and beneath them are felt as turbulence, and the precipitation falls as showers, meaning heavy and intermittent rather than steady. PHAK Ch. 12 pairs unstable/moist with cumuliform clouds, turbulence, showery precipitation and good visibility.

Wrong. Poor visibility with smooth air is the signature of a moist STABLE air mass: stratiform clouds, fog and steady drizzle, with no vertical mixing to bump the aircraft or clear the air. It is a correct weather description attached to the wrong stability.

Wrong. Haze and smoke are also stable-air traits. Without vertical motion, pollutants and particulates stay trapped near the surface; unstable air mixes them upward and typically leaves visibility good. Same error as option B, with the visibility restriction named instead of described.
Unstable means cumuliform clouds, turbulence, showery precipitation and good visibility; stable means stratiform clouds, smooth air, steady drizzle and poor visibility.
FAA-H-8083-25 PHAK Ch. 12 (Weather Theory), atmospheric stability and air masses; FAA-H-8083-28 Aviation Weather Handbook, stability; FAA-G-8082-22 Remote Pilot Study Guide (weather)
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
All three options are genuine air-mass descriptions; B and C both belong to STABLE air.
