UA.I.B.K16
According to 14 CFR part 107, how may a remote pilot operate an unmanned aircraft in Class C airspace?
The remote pilot must have prior authorization from the Air Traffic Control (ATC) facility having jurisdiction over that airspace.
The remote pilot must monitor the Air Traffic Control (ATC) frequency from launch to recovery.
The remote pilot must contact the Air Traffic Control (ATC) facility after launching the unmanned aircraft.

14 CFR 107.41 says no person may operate a small UA in Class B, C, or D airspace, or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E designated for an airport, unless that person has PRIOR authorization from ATC. The word that decides this question is "prior" — authorization has to exist before the flight, normally via LAANC or a DroneZone request. Part 107 imposes no radio-monitoring requirement, and calling ATC after launch is exactly backwards.

Correct. 14 CFR 107.41 states that no person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in Class B, Class C, or Class D airspace, or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport, unless that person has prior authorization from ATC. "Prior" is the operative word: the authorization, normally through LAANC or a DroneZone request, has to be in hand before launch.

Wrong because it imports a manned-aircraft habit into part 107. Part 107 contains no requirement to carry, tune, or monitor a radio at all, and listening to a frequency is not an authorization, so a remote pilot could monitor ATC from launch to recovery and still be in violation of 107.41.

Wrong on timing. 107.41 requires the authorization before the operation, so a flight that launches first and calls afterward was unauthorized the moment it left the ground, and ATC has no mechanism to retroactively approve an operation already underway.
Class B, C, D, or a Class E surface area means you need the ATC authorization in hand before you launch, not during and not after.
14 CFR 107.41, Operation in certain airspace
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-B/section-107.41

UA.II.A.K1b
According to 14 CFR part 107 the remote pilot in command (PIC) of a small unmanned aircraft planning to operate within Class C airspace
must use a visual observer.
is required to file a flight plan.
is required to receive ATC authorization.

Same rule as question 2: 107.41 requires ATC authorization for Class C. A visual observer is optional under part 107 (107.33 permits one but never requires one; the remote PIC only needs to maintain visual line of sight themselves). Flight plans are an instrument/VFR manned-aviation concept and part 107 has no flight-plan requirement at all.

Wrong: a visual observer is optional under part 107, never mandatory. 107.33 only describes how a VO must be used if the remote PIC chooses to use one, and 107.31 puts the visual line of sight duty on the remote PIC or the person manipulating the controls, so no rule forces a VO because the airspace is Class C.

Wrong: part 107 has no flight plan provision anywhere in it. Flight plans are a part 91 manned-aviation item (required for IFR, voluntary for VFR), and the part 107 entry ticket to controlled airspace is an ATC authorization, not a filed plan.

Correct. 14 CFR 107.41 prohibits small UA operations in Class B, Class C, or Class D airspace, or within the lateral boundaries of a Class E surface area for an airport, without prior ATC authorization, so Class C requires that authorization (typically obtained through LAANC).
Controlled airspace under part 107 costs you one thing: an ATC authorization. Not a flight plan, not a visual observer.
14 CFR 107.41; see also 14 CFR 107.31 and 107.33
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-B/section-107.41

UA.III.B.K1a
What effect does high density altitude have on the efficiency of a UA propeller?
Propeller efficiency is increased.
Propeller efficiency is decreased.
Density altitude does not affect propeller efficiency.

A propeller is an airfoil that produces thrust by accelerating a mass of air rearward. High density altitude means thin air, so each revolution moves less mass and generates less thrust, and engine power drops at the same time. The common trap is thinking thin air means less drag on the blades and therefore better performance — the loss of air mass to work on dominates, so efficiency and thrust both fall.
FAA-H-8083-25 Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Ch. 4/11 (density altitude and performance)

Wrong, and this is the backwards-intuition answer. Students reason that thinner air means less resistance on the blades, so the prop must spin more freely and work better. Thrust depends on the mass of air the blades accelerate rearward, and thin air supplies less of it, so efficiency cannot go up.

Correct. A propeller is a rotating airfoil, and high density altitude (hot, high, humid) means fewer air molecules per cubic foot, so each blade produces less thrust at the same RPM and blade angle. The PHAK performance discussion lists decreased propeller efficiency alongside reduced power output as paired effects of high density altitude.

Wrong: density altitude is the single biggest environmental driver of aircraft performance. The PHAK ties high density altitude directly to reduced power, reduced propeller efficiency, reduced lift, and longer takeoff distances, so "no effect" contradicts the handbook outright.
High density altitude means thin air, and thin air means less power, less lift, less thrust, and a less efficient propeller.
FAA-H-8083-25 Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Ch. 4 (Principles of Flight) and Ch. 11 (Aircraft Performance), density altitude effects
https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Thin air really does reduce drag on the blades, but the lost air mass to accelerate wins, so efficiency drops.

UA.V.B.K6a
(Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 22, area 2.) At Coeur D'Alene which frequency should be used as a Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF) to monitor airport traffic?

Coeur d'Alene (COE, Pappy Boyington Field) is non-towered and its charted CTAF/UNICOM is 122.8 MHz, printed on the sectional next to a solid magenta circled "C". The two distractors are the other frequencies printed in that same area of the chart: 135.075 is the AWOS-3 weather broadcast, and 122.05 is a Boise Radio (Flight Service) remote outlet, neither of which carries airport traffic advisories. The trap is grabbing any nearby number instead of the one flagged by the circled C.
FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide (airport data block, CTAF circled-C symbol); FAA Chart Supplement / airport facility data for KCOE (CTAF/UNICOM 122.8, AWOS-3 135.075, Boise Radio 122.05)
Figure 22, area 2

Wrong: 122.05 is charted in that area as a remote communications outlet for the Flight Service Station (Boise Radio), which on a sectional appears as a frequency printed above or beside a boxed FSS name, not inside the airport data block. Flight Service gives briefings and relays clearances; it does not carry self-announced airport traffic at this field.

Wrong: 135.075 is the automated weather broadcast at Coeur d'Alene (AWOS-3). In the airport data block weather frequencies are tagged AWOS or ASOS, they transmit a recorded observation only, and no pilot announces position or intentions on them.

UA.I.B.K14a
Which technique should a remote pilot use to scan for traffic? A remote pilot should
systematically focus on different segments of the sky for short intervals.
concentrate on relative movement detected in the peripheral vision area.
continuously scan the sky from right to left.

The eye can only resolve detail in the narrow foveal region and needs roughly a second of fixation to focus, so effective scanning means dividing the sky into small blocks and pausing on each one in a systematic sequence. Peripheral vision detects movement but cannot identify or resolve an aircraft, and a continuous sweep never lets the eye stop and focus, so distant traffic simply never registers. The trap is that a smooth continuous sweep feels more thorough while actually seeing less.
AIM 8-1-6 (Vision in Flight, scanning for other aircraft); FAA-H-8083-25 Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Ch. 14 (collision avoidance)

Correct. AIM 8-1-6 says eye movements should not exceed about 10 degrees and each area should be observed for at least one second to enable detection, which is precisely a systematic series of short fixations on small segments of sky rather than one continuous motion.

Wrong because it inverts how the eye actually works. Peripheral vision is good at catching motion but has poor resolving power and cannot identify an aircraft or judge its closure, and the genuinely dangerous aircraft (one on a collision course) shows almost no relative movement at all.

Wrong: a smooth continuous sweep gives the eye nothing to lock onto. Without a stop of roughly a second the image never resolves on the fovea, so a continuous right-to-left scan can pass directly over converging traffic and register nothing.
Scan in short stops, roughly 10-degree blocks held about a second each, never in a smooth sweep.

https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap8_section_1.html

47 pounds.
38 pounds.

Wrong: 47 pounds is 33 x 1.41, and 1.41 G is the 45-degree bank value. This is the classic one-step error on the bank angle axis, made worse because 1.41 G at 45 degrees is a figure students memorize and then apply to the wrong bank.

Figure 2 plots exactly that curve, so enter the bottom axis at 30 degrees, read up to the curve, and get about 1.15 G. 33 lb x 1.154 = 38.1 lb, which rounds to 38 pounds.

A local TV station has hired a remote pilot to operate their small UA to cover news stories. The remote pilot has had multiple near misses with obstacles on the ground and two small UAS accidents. What would be a solution for the news station to improve their operating safety culture?
The news station should implement a policy of no more than five crashes/incidents within 6 months.
The news station does not need to make any changes; there are times that an accident is unavoidable.
The news station should recognize hazardous attitudes and situations and develop standard operating procedures that emphasize safety.

A safety culture is built by identifying hazards and hazardous attitudes and then writing standard operating procedures that make the safe action the default, which is exactly what the pattern of near misses and accidents calls for. Setting a tolerated crash quota institutionalizes the hazard instead of removing it, and declaring accidents unavoidable is the Resignation attitude dressed up as policy. (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 26, area 2.) While monitoring the Cooperstown CTAF you hear an aircraft announce that they are midfield left downwind to RWY 13. Where would the aircraft be relative to the runway?
The aircraft is East.
The aircraft is South.
The aircraft is West.

Runway 13 means a landing heading of about 130 degrees, so downwind is flown on the reciprocal, about 310 degrees. "Left downwind" means the runway lies off the aircraft's left wing, which at a 310-degree heading is a bearing of about 220 degrees from the aircraft — putting the aircraft roughly northeast of the runway, and East is the only option in that half of the compass. The trap is reading left and right from the ground observer's point of view instead of from the cockpit.

Figure 26, area 2

Correct: work it in three steps, no chart needed. Runway number times 10 is the landing direction (13 = 130 degrees); downwind is flown on the reciprocal (310 degrees); and 'left' downwind means the runway sits off the pilot's LEFT wing, which from a 310-degree heading is a bearing of about 220 degrees. If the runway is 220 degrees from the aircraft, the aircraft is 040 degrees from the runway, i.e. northeast, and East is the only option in that half of the compass (AIM 4-3-3).

Wrong: South is where you land if you confuse the direction the runway POINTS with where the traffic is. Runway 13 points southeast, but downwind is a leg flown parallel to and offset from the runway, not off either end, so an answer on the extended centerline cannot describe a midfield downwind (AIM 4-3-3, standard rectangular pattern).

Wrong: West is the left/right reversal. A RIGHT downwind to RWY 13 would put the aircraft on the southwest side, and you get that answer either by ignoring the word 'left' or by judging left and right from a ground observer facing the aircraft instead of from the cockpit. In the AIM pattern, 'left' always means left turns and runway off the pilot's left wing.
Downwind heading is the reciprocal of the runway heading, and 'left downwind' puts the runway off the pilot's left wing, so the aircraft sits on the opposite side.

(Refer to Figure 26, area 1.) The magenta hatched boundary labelled DEVILS LAKE EAST MOA crosses the area. May a remote pilot operate a small UAS inside an active MOA?
Only with a waiver of § 107.45
Yes. No regulation prohibits it, but military aircraft may be manoeuvring at high speed, so exercise extreme caution
No. MOAs are prohibited to civil aircraft while active

A MOA is not restricted airspace. It separates military training from IFR traffic; VFR and small UAS operations are permitted. The hazard is real, fast aircraft, so check activation times with Flight Service and keep a visual observer busy. § 107.45 covers prohibited and restricted areas, not MOAs.
FAA-CT-8080-2H Figure 26; AIM 3-4-5
Figure 26, area 1
§ 107.45 applies to prohibited and restricted areas. A MOA needs no waiver and no permission.
Correct. MOAs do not exclude civil VFR or part 107 operations; the chart margin and Flight Service tell you when they are active so you can judge the hazard.
MOAs restrict IFR traffic routing, not VFR or small UAS. Prohibition applies to P- areas, and permission is needed for R- areas.
MOA: permitted, but military traffic may be manoeuvring. Check activation and keep clear.
AIM 3-4-5, Military Operations Areas

UA.II.A.K1d

(Refer to Figure 26, area 4.) Jamestown Regional is a magenta airport inside a dashed magenta box, with a magenta vignette around that. You plan to fly at 250 ft AGL, 2 miles from the runway and inside the dashed box. What applies?
Class G below 700 ft: no authorization is needed because the airport is magenta
Class D: authorization is required because of the ASOS
Class E surface area: ATC authorization is required even though the airport has no tower

Read the line, not the airport colour. The dashed magenta box is a Class E surface area, which § 107.41 lists alongside B, C and D. The vignette outside the box marks where Class E begins at 700 ft AGL instead, and below that vignette, outside the box, you are in Class G with no authorization needed.
FAA-CT-8080-2H Figure 26; 14 CFR 107.41
Figure 26, area 4
Class G below 700 ft applies under the vignette, outside the dashed box. Inside the box the controlled airspace reaches the ground.
Class D needs an operating control tower and is drawn with dashed blue. An ASOS is weather equipment.
Correct. Inside the dashed magenta box, Class E starts at the surface and § 107.41 applies. The lack of a tower changes nothing.
Dashed magenta box around a magenta airport: Class E surface area, authorization required.
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-B/section-107.41
Assuming non-towered means uncontrolled.

UA.II.X.C1
(Refer to Figure 26, area 4.) A dashed magenta line labelled 5°E runs north to south west of Jamestown. A flight plan gives a true course of 090°. What is the magnetic course?
090°, because variation does not apply to drones

East is least. The isogonic line shows magnetic variation. With 5° east variation, magnetic equals true minus 5°, so 090° true is 085° magnetic. West variation is added. A sectional's VOR compass roses are already oriented to magnetic north.
FAA-CT-8080-2H Figure 26; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide
Figure 26, area 4
Correct. 5°E variation: subtract. 090° true becomes 085° magnetic. East is least, west is best.
Adding is for west variation. This line reads 5°E.
Variation is a property of the Earth's magnetic field, not of the aircraft. Any magnetic compass, including the one in a drone, sees it.
Isogonic line gives variation: east is least (subtract), west is best (add).
Aeronautical Chart User's Guide, Isogonic lines
https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav/digital_products/aero_guide/
Adding east variation.

UA.II.A.K1b

(Refer to Figure 23, area 3.) The outer ring of the Savannah Class C is marked 41/13 and the inner ring 41/SFC. You are under the outer ring, 8 miles from the airport, at 300 ft AGL over terrain of about 40 ft MSL. Is ATC authorization required for the Class C?
Yes, because 41 means the Class C begins at 41 ft AGL
No. The outer ring's floor is 1,300 ft MSL and you are far below it, so you are not in Class C; check for any surface area that does reach the ground
Yes. Class C is a single column from the surface wherever the rings are drawn

Read the fraction. The top number is the ceiling and the bottom is the floor, both in hundreds of feet MSL. 41/13 means 4,100 ft MSL down to 1,300 ft MSL. At roughly 340 ft MSL you are beneath the shelf, in whatever airspace lies below it. 41/SFC, the inner ring, is the part that reaches the surface. Always still check for a Class D or Class E surface area under the shelf.
FAA-CT-8080-2H Figure 23; 14 CFR 107.41
Figure 23, area 3
The numbers are hundreds of feet MSL: 41 is 4,100 ft, the ceiling. The floor is the lower number, 13, 1,300 ft MSL.
Correct. The outer shelf floor is 1,300 ft MSL; 300 ft AGL over 40 ft terrain is about 340 ft MSL, well under it. The Class C does not reach you there.
Class C is tiered. Only the inner ring, marked SFC, reaches the surface. The outer ring is a shelf with a floor.
Class C fractions: ceiling over floor, hundreds of feet MSL; SFC means the ring reaches the ground.
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-B/section-107.41
Treating the outer shelf as surface-based airspace.

UA.II.X.C4
(Refer to Figure 23, area 3.) Southwest of Savannah an obstruction is printed as 1548 with (1534) beneath it. Approximately what is the ground elevation at its base?
About 1,534 ft MSL
About 3,082 ft MSL
About 14 ft MSL

MSL top minus AGL height equals ground elevation. 1,548 minus 1,534 is 14 ft MSL, which fits the coastal Georgia terrain. The tall symbol confirms the structure is over 1,000 ft AGL. This is the arithmetic you need to convert your 400 ft AGL limit to an MSL altitude on a chart.
FAA-CT-8080-2H Figure 23; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide
Figure 23, area 3
1,534 is the height of the structure above the ground, not the ground's elevation.
Adding the two numbers has no meaning. Subtract to get the base elevation.
Correct. Subtract the parenthetical AGL height from the bold MSL top: 1,548 minus 1,534 is about 14 ft MSL at the base.
Ground elevation at an obstruction equals its MSL top minus its AGL height.
Aeronautical Chart User's Guide, Obstructions
https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav/digital_products/aero_guide/
Adding instead of subtracting, or reading the parenthetical as MSL.
